title: A Sneaky, Hidden Reason Why You're Inconsistent https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2018/06/02/a-sneaky-hidden-reason-why-youre-inconsistent/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes discovering, through personal coaching sessions with teachers who already knew SCM's principles well, a hidden cause of inconsistency he had never directly addressed: teachers were unsure exactly what did and didn't count as breaking their own rules. He illustrates this with examples—a student calling out a good answer, quiet talking during transitions, a student getting up for a tissue—where teachers hesitated because enforcement felt awkward or nitpicky in the moment. This uncertainty, he explains, caused teachers to freeze and do nothing, which then opened the door to escalating misbehavior. His solution is for teachers to decide, well before the school year begins, exactly what each rule means in practice and to eliminate all gray area, including any narrowly defined and clearly taught exceptions. Once the boundaries are fixed in the teacher's own mind, he argues, consistent enforcement becomes far easier.
points: A hidden cause of inconsistency is not knowing precisely what does and doesn't constitute breaking one's own posted rules.
Ambiguous situations—like calling out a good answer or quiet talk during transitions—cause teachers to hesitate and then do nothing.
Not knowing where the line is leads teachers to freeze, which then invites more serious misbehavior.
The fix is deciding ahead of time, before the school year starts, exactly what each rule means in the teacher's specific classroom.
Any exceptions to a rule must be narrowly defined and explicitly taught so students know exactly where the boundaries are.
quotes: They were unsure what did and didn’t constitute breaking their own rules.
It didn’t feel right in the moment to enforce a consequence, but technically it was against the rules.

Not knowing where the line was caused these teachers to freeze, question themselves, and then, more often than not, do nothing at all—which inevitably would lead to other, more serious and disruptive behaviors.
The solution is to decide ahead of time exactly what is and isn’t okay, and then teach and model what that looks like to students.
You must be clear in your own mind where the boundary lines are before you can ever effectively teach them to your students or enforce them consistently.
Once your boundaries are clearly established, and non-negotiably set in stone, all awkwardness and indecision will disappear.
